title: Extensibility & Open-Closed Architectures

topics.title: Refactoring Giant Switch/If-Else Chains
topics.description: Techniques to replace hardcoded procedural switch-case chains with polymorphic strategy dispatch.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Replacing monolithic switch(type) statements with polymorphic class hierarchies or strategy maps.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Switch chains violate the Open/Closed Principle: every new feature requires modifying every switch block across the entire project.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Extract each case block into a standalone class implementing a shared interface.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Use a factory or registry map to dispatch to the correct class polymorphically.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Before vs After
callout.text: Before: switch(type) { case PDF: ... case CSV: ... case JSON: ... } (Bloated)\nAfter: exporterMap[type]->exportData() (Extensible!)

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ReportExportRegistry replaces switch statements with dynamic hash map dispatch.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Payment processors, document exporters, game command handlers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use whenever you see duplicate switch(enum) statements scattered across multiple files.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not replace simple 2-case switches for static state.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Zero switch maintenance; new formats registered at runtime.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Small hash map lookup indirection.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Map of Strategies, Factory Pattern, Polymorphic Subclasses.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Leaving default switch cases that throw runtime errors when new enums are added.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is switch-case over an enum considered a code smell in object-oriented design?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because adding a new enum value requires searching and editing every switch block across the entire codebase, violating OCP and risking unhandled cases.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor renderShape(ShapeType) switch to shape->render().

referenceCode.code: class IShape { public: virtual void render() = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Refactoring Giant Switch/If-Else Chains is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Plugin & Registry Architectures in C++
topics.description: Designing dynamic self-registering plugin architectures using static initialization and factory maps.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A Plugin Registry allows new classes to automatically register themselves with a central factory at startup without modifying the factory source code.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Adding a new plugin should not require modifying the central factory's switch statement.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Self-registering static proxies register creator functions into a central map during static initialization.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: REGISTER_PLUGIN(CsvExporter, "csv") automatically registers the class before main() runs.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Self-Registration Macro
callout.text: static bool registered = PluginFactory::registerCreator("pdf", []{ return make_unique<PdfPlugin>(); });

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: AudioPlugin self-registers into PluginFactory before main() executes.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Photoshop filters, Audio DAW VSTs, Database dialect plugins in ORMs.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when building extensible software frameworks where 3rd parties can add new plugins.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not rely on static registration across static library (.a / .lib) boundaries without linker include flags.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: True 100% decoupling: adding a plugin requires zero edits to core engine files.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Static initialization order subtleties across shared libraries.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Dynamic DLL/so loading via dlopen/LoadLibrary, Static Registry.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Static initialization order fiasco when registry map is initialized after plugins.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does self-registration work during static initialization in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A static global or static inline boolean variable in the plugin's .cpp file initializes before main() runs, calling the central factory's registration method.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build self-registering driver framework for Postgres and MySQL.

sections.content: Mastering Plugin & Registry Architectures in C++ is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Case Study: Multi-Gateway Extensible Payment Engine
topics.description: End-to-end architectural case study refactoring a monolithic payment engine into an open-closed extensible system.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A comprehensive case study applying SOLID, Strategy, Factory, and Dependency Injection to architect a multi-gateway payment engine.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Payment systems must support credit cards, PayPal, Apple Pay, Crypto, and regional gateways without modifying checkout workflows.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Decouple checkout orchestrator from payment execution strategies and gateway adapters.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Gateway Registry + Strategy Pattern + Invariant Validation.

sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: PaymentEngine orchestrates payment strategies dynamically with zero hardcoded switch blocks.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: E-commerce platforms (Shopify, Amazon), SaaS subscription billing engines (Stripe Billing).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use in any multi-provider integration architecture.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if only one fixed payment provider is supported.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: 100% Open/Closed; seamless gateway onboarding.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires robust error translation from 3rd-party gateway error codes.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Synchronous Payment Engine, Asynchronous Webhook Payment Engine.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Hardcoding currency conversion logic inside individual gateway classes.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How do you handle gateway-specific configuration (e.g. API keys) in an extensible payment engine?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Pass gateway-specific configuration objects to concrete strategy constructors during initialization or factory assembly, keeping the shared IPaymentStrategy interface clean and generic.
